The story became ____6____ to follow when we made the two voices different. We also decided ____7____ a short pause after each question, giving the other character time to answer. The teacher listened and helped us shorten one long sentence.

The labels for our sound collection

Shared bank: ask | but | careful | easy | for | inform | make | member | they | two

Last month, our music club ____1____ a collection of everyday sounds. We recorded a closing door, footsteps and water being poured. A teacher checked the plan and made sure we did not record private conversations.

Several ____2____ worked in pairs. One used the equipment while the other wrote down what was being recorded. We gave every file a short label, but the first names were not very ____3____. “Sound1” told us nothing about its contents.

We renamed the files ____4____ so that the object and date were visible. Then we compared ____5____ with our notes. Two recordings had been given each other's labels. Listening again let us correct the mistake before the files were shared.

This was the ____6____ check, after an earlier check of the recording quality. The teacher explained that a clear recording with a wrong label could still mislead the listener. We were checking different parts of the same task.

The new list was ____7____ to use than the first one. The teacher suggested ____8____ one person to check the final order while someone else followed the notes. It did not take long, ____9____ it gave us another chance to notice a missing item.

When the class listened to the collection, they guessed what had made each sound. We did not show the descriptive labels until afterwards. The activity worked because the hidden answers were kept separate from the public order. We thanked the teacher ____10____ helping us build a collection that was not only interesting to hear but also possible to understand and reuse later.

The route described from memory

Shared bank: borrow | clear | describe | independent | judge | mistake | participate | precise | preserve | tropical | trust | use

In a fictional town project, students asked residents to describe a familiar journey without looking at a map. One man began with the bakery that had closed years before. His ____1____ was still clear to him, even though the building now held another business.

We initially replaced the old name in our notes with the current one. Our teacher asked us to consider what the interview was meant to ____2____. If it recorded a remembered journey, removing the old landmark could erase part of that memory. If it guided present-day visitors, the current name would be more ____3____.

The two purposes did not require one version to be treated as a ____4____. They required us to identify what each account was doing. We kept the resident's wording in the interview record and added a separate note about the present location. The note was ____5____ distinguished from his speech.

Several ____6____ offered different names for the same corner. We did not silently combine them into a single quotation. Instead, we recorded whose description used which name and when the interviews took place. The differences became something to investigate rather than an inconvenience to hide.

Our final display was ____7____ than the first draft because readers could see both the remembered route and its relation to the current town. Another group checked the references ____8____ before publication. One uncertain location was left unresolved, not placed at the nearest convenient street.

The project did not produce a perfect navigation tool. It produced a record of how people described a place through memory. Preserving those limits made the account more ____9____. A useful map of memory could keep its personal detail while giving readers enough context to make their own ____10____.

We compared the new masks with ____5____ in the first photographs. This was the ____6____ full review after an earlier review of comfort and fit. Each check answered a different question. Passing one did not mean the whole object was ready.

The revised patterns were ____7____ to recognise than before. The teacher suggested ____8____ them under the actual stage lighting too. A colour that looked strong at the table might appear different from the audience seats.

The extra check took time, ____9____ it prevented a surprise during the performance. We still kept the actor's safe movement as the first concern. At the end, we thanked the teacher ____10____ helping us see the masks from more than one position. A stage object belonged partly to the person wearing it and partly to the audience's view. In a fictional museum project, our class reviewed a self-guided tour. Its map led visitors through five rooms, but a sixth room was not mentioned. Some pupils assumed the omission showed that its contents were ____1____. A staff member explained that the room was temporarily closed for necessary work.

The absence from the route reflected access, not a judgement of historical value. Our teacher asked us to keep that ____2____ clear in the review. We could criticise the missing explanation without inventing a motive for the omission.

The museum added a short note naming the closed room and explaining the current arrangement. The wording was ____3____ visible beside the route map. It did not promise a reopening date that staff could not yet ____4____. Visitors were directed to current information instead.

Several ____5____ said the note helped them understand the gap. One still wanted more information about the room's contents, which was a different request. The museum considered whether a separate page could provide that material without presenting old images as a current view.

Our revised review was ____6____ than the first. We distinguished what the route offered, what was unavailable and what remained a suggestion. A partner checked every factual statement ____7____ against the supplied information.

The project showed how easily an unexplained blank can invite a confident story. Sometimes that story may be right; here it was not supported. Asking a specific question had produced a more ____8____ account. We did not need to defend every museum choice in order to describe this one fairly. A useful review could be both critical and ____9____, leaving readers able to follow its reasons. The missing room had not ended the tour. It had changed the questions we needed to ask about the route's ____10____.
